cards.name: Afghanistan
cards.story: Unified in 1747 under Ahmad Shah Durrani, Afghanistan's borders were imposed through 19th-century Anglo-Afghan Wars and British-Russian 'Great Game' treaties—including the 1893 Durand Line dividing Pashtun communities—while Emir Abdur Rahman Khan's 1890s subjugation of Hazarajat killed or displaced over half the Hazara population. After winning full independence from Britain in 1919, the Soviet–Afghan War (1979–89) killed an estimated 1 to 2 million Afghans and drove over 5 million into exile, followed by post-2001 warfare that caused over 170,000 direct deaths and displaced millions more.
cards.contestedNote: The 1893 Durand Line separating Afghanistan and Pakistan divides ethnic Pashtun communities and has long been politically sensitive.

cards.name: Albania
cards.story: After nearly five centuries of Ottoman rule, Albania declared independence in 1912 during the Balkan Wars, in which invading Balkan armies killed tens of thousands of Albanian civilians and displaced hundreds of thousands. Major European powers drew Albania's borders at the 1913 London Conference, leaving nearly half of all ethnic Albanians outside the state in neighboring Kosovo and Macedonia.

cards.name: Algeria
cards.story: France invaded Algeria in 1830 and waged decades of scorched-earth conquest and engineered famine that killed an estimated 500,000 to 1 million Algerians while seizing fertile land for European settlers. During the 1954–62 War of Independence, French forces killed hundreds of thousands of Algerians (estimates range from 250,000–400,000 in French scholarship to 1.5 million in Algerian counts) and forcibly interned roughly 2 million rural civilians in regroupment camps before the 1962 Évian Accords ended colonial rule and roughly 900,000 European settlers and Harkis fled.

cards.name: Andorra
cards.story: Tucked high in the Pyrenees mountains, Andorra preserved its borders through the 1278 Act of Paréage, splitting feudal sovereignty between the Bishop of Urgell in Spain and a French count (later France's President). Though spared direct war, it served as an escape corridor for thousands of refugees fleeing the Spanish Civil War and Nazi-occupied Europe during World War II.

cards.name: Angola
cards.story: Portuguese colonizers turned Angola and the Kongo coast into the largest single source of the transatlantic slave trade, forcibly trafficking over 4 million enslaved Africans across the Atlantic before European treaties in the 1880s carved Angola across historic kingdoms. After a 13-year anti-colonial war won independence in 1975, a 27-year Cold War–fueled civil war killed an estimated 500,000 to 800,000 people and displaced roughly 4 million.

cards.name: Antigua & Barbuda
cards.story: English colonizers seized Antigua in 1632, displacing Indigenous Kalinago people and building a brutal sugar plantation colony powered by over 100,000 enslaved Africans—while turning Barbuda into a private estate for the Codrington family before merging both islands in 1860. After centuries of colonial rule and resistance, Antigua and Barbuda gained full independence from Britain in 1981.

cards.name: Argentina
cards.story: Breaking from Spanish colonial rule in 1816, Argentina forged its vast southern borders through the 1870s–80s 'Conquest of the Desert'—a military campaign that killed thousands of Indigenous Mapuche, Tehuelche, and Ranquel people, enslaved or displaced tens of thousands more, and fixed the 1881 Andes border with Chile. Earlier, Argentina joined Brazil and Uruguay in the War of the Triple Alliance against Paraguay, and its 1976–83 military dictatorship later murdered or 'disappeared' an estimated 30,000 people.

cards.name: Armenia
cards.story: With over 2,500 years of history across the Armenian Highlands, Armenia's modern borders were shaped in the aftermath of the 1915–23 Armenian Genocide, in which the Ottoman Empire murdered an estimated 1 to 1.5 million Armenians and drove hundreds of thousands from ancestral Western Armenia. Briefly independent in 1918 before Soviet annexation in 1920, Armenia became independent upon the USSR's 1991 collapse; decades of conflict with Azerbaijan culminated in September 2023, when Azerbaijan's military offensive forced over 100,000 ethnic Armenians—nearly the entire population of Nagorno-Karabakh—to flee to Armenia.
cards.contestedNote: Armenia and Azerbaijan continue border demarcation talks following wars over Nagorno-Karabakh that displaced roughly 700,000 Azerbaijanis in the 1990s and over 100,000 ethnic Armenians in September 2023.

cards.name: Australia
cards.story: Home to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples for over 60,000 years (an estimated 1 to 1.5 million people in 1788), Britain claimed the continent as 'terra nullius' ('nobody's land') and forged six colonies through violent Frontier Wars—with researchers documenting over 10,300 Indigenous deaths across 400+ massacres and tens of thousands killed overall alongside epidemic collapse that reduced the Indigenous population by ~75–90%. After federating in 1901, Australian governments also forcibly removed tens of thousands of Indigenous children ('Stolen Generations') into the 1970s.

cards.name: Austria
cards.story: Once the core of the Austro-Hungarian Empire, Austria was reduced to its modern German-speaking borders after World War I killed over 1.2 million Austro-Hungarian soldiers. After Nazi Germany annexed Austria (Anschluss) in 1938, the regime murdered roughly 65,000 Austrian Jews and drove ~130,000 into exile during the Holocaust before Allied occupation ended with the 1955 Austrian State Treaty.

cards.name: Azerbaijan
cards.story: Conquered by the Russian Empire in the early 1800s and briefly independent in 1918–20 before Soviet Red Army invasion, Azerbaijan regained independence along Soviet borders—including the Nakhchivan exclave—in 1991. The First Nagorno-Karabakh War (1988–94) killed over 30,000 people and displaced roughly 700,000 Azerbaijanis and hundreds of thousands of Armenians, before Azerbaijan's 2020 war and 2023 offensive retook Nagorno-Karabakh and triggered the flight of over 100,000 ethnic Armenians.
cards.contestedNote: After decades of conflict that displaced ~700,000 Azerbaijanis in the 1990s and over 100,000 ethnic Armenians in 2023, Azerbaijan retook Nagorno-Karabakh while formal border demarcation with Armenia continues.

cards.name: Bahamas
cards.story: Originally home to an estimated 40,000 Indigenous Lucayan Taíno people, the Bahamas was completely depopulated within 30 years of Christopher Columbus's 1492 landing through Spanish slave raids and Old World epidemics. English settlers arrived in 1648 and King Charles II granted the islands to the Lords Proprietors in 1670 before Britain suppressed piracy, established a Crown Colony in 1718, and imported thousands of enslaved Africans—many brought by Loyalists after the American Revolution—until independence in 1973.

cards.name: Bahrain
cards.story: Conquered by the Al Khalifa family from Persian control in 1783, Bahrain entered British protection treaties in the 1800s that secured British imperial influence over Gulf shipping and oil. After Britain withdrew in 1971, Bahrain chose separate independence rather than joining the UAE; political protests—including the 2011 Arab Spring uprising—were met with security crackdowns and Gulf military intervention that killed dozens and jailed thousands.

cards.name: Bangladesh
cards.story: Britain's 1947 Partition of India split historic Bengal, turning its eastern half into 'East Pakistan,' 1,000 miles across India from West Pakistan, amid mass displacement of millions of Bengalis. When West Pakistan's military launched Operation Searchlight in March 1971 to crush Bengali self-determination, the nine-month Liberation War and mass atrocities killed an estimated 300,000 to 500,000+ people in independent demographic counts (up to 3 million in official Bangladeshi figures, plus over 500,000 excess deaths among refugees) and forced roughly 10 million refugees into India before Bangladesh won independence.

cards.name: Barbados
cards.story: Claimed by England in 1625 and held continuously until 1966, Barbados became the prototype of Britain's Caribbean slave-sugar complex: colonizers trafficked an estimated 400,000 to 600,000 enslaved Africans onto the tiny island under the harsh 1661 Slave Code, crushing uprisings such as Bussa's 1816 rebellion. Barbados gained independence in 1966 and became a republic in 2021.

cards.name: Belarus
cards.story: Stalin's 1939 Soviet invasion of eastern Poland expanded Soviet Belarus westward, deporting hundreds of thousands of Poles and Belarusians to Siberia. During World War II, Nazi Germany's brutal occupation destroyed over 9,200 villages across Belarus—burning 628 villages such as Khatyn together with their entire populations—and killed roughly 2.2 to 2.3 million people (around 25% of Belarus's pre-war population, including ~600,000 to 800,000 Belarusian Jews) before those Soviet republic lines became independent Belarus's borders in 1991.

cards.name: Belgium
cards.story: Belgium broke from the United Kingdom of the Netherlands in 1830 and finalized its European borders in the 1839 Treaty of London, later suffering brutal German occupations in both World Wars (including ~25,000 Jews murdered in the Holocaust). Overseas, Belgium's King Leopold II and colonial state ruled the Congo, Rwanda, and Burundi—where forced labor, terror, disease, and famine in the Congo Free State alone caused an estimated 1.5 to 10 million population loss among Congolese people.

cards.name: Belize
cards.story: Built around British mahogany and logwood camps on ancestral Maya lands, Britain imported enslaved Africans and violently expelled Maya villages during the 19th-century Caste War spillover, naming the colony British Honduras until 1973. Belize gained independence in 1981 while neighboring Guatemala maintained a territorial claim over its southern half.
cards.contestedNote: Guatemala and Belize agreed to submit Guatemala's long-standing colonial-era territorial claim over southern Belize to the International Court of Justice.

cards.name: Benin
cards.story: Before France conquered the Kingdom of Dahomey in 1892–94 and forced diverse northern and southern peoples into one colony, the Bight of Benin was one of the hardest-hit zones of the transatlantic slave trade, with roughly 2 million people trafficked from its coast. Independent since 1960 along French colonial borders, the country renamed itself Benin in 1975.

cards.name: Bhutan
cards.story: Unified in the 1600s and never colonized by a European empire, Bhutan lost fertile southern Duar plains to British India in the 1864–65 Duar War before the Treaty of Sinchula fixed its southern border. While its Himalayan monarchy preserved sovereignty from 1907 onward, state assimilation policies and citizenship revocations in the late 1980s and 1990s forcibly expelled roughly 100,000 ethnic Nepali Lhotshampa citizens—about one-sixth of Bhutan's population—into refugee camps in Nepal.

cards.name: Bolivia
cards.story: Conquered by Spain in the 1530s, Bolivia's Potosí silver mines used the brutal mita forced-labor system over nearly three centuries, contributing to millions of Indigenous Andean deaths from exhaustion, mercury poisoning, and epidemics. Independent in 1825, Bolivia lost its Pacific coastline to Chile in the War of the Pacific (1879–84) and southeastern lowlands in the 1932–35 Chaco War—which killed ~55,000–65,000 Bolivian soldiers.

cards.name: Bosnia & Herzegovina
cards.story: Declaring independence during Yugoslavia's breakup in 1992, Bosnia and Herzegovina endured a 3.5-year war marked by systematic ethnic cleansing and the 1995 Srebrenica genocide, in which Bosnian Serb forces executed over 8,000 Bosniak men and boys and expelled ~30,000 women and children. Overall, the war killed roughly 100,000 people and forcibly displaced ~2 million—half the pre-war population—before the 1995 Dayton Accords froze its borders and internal political divisions.
cards.contestedNote: Bosnia's outer borders are internationally recognized, though the Dayton Accords divided internal governance along wartime ethnic cleansing lines that displaced ~2 million people.

cards.name: Botswana
cards.story: In 1885, Tswana leaders accepted British protection as the Bechuanaland Protectorate to resist violent land seizure by Cecil Rhodes's colonial company and neighboring white-settler republics. Even under British rule and later independence in 1966, Indigenous San (Basarwa) communities faced long-term dispossession and forced relocations from ancestral lands in the Central Kalahari.

cards.name: Brazil
cards.story: Portuguese colonizers invaded Brazil in 1500, driving a collapse of Indigenous populations (from an estimated 2–5 million to a few hundred thousand through conquest, forced labor, and epidemics) and trafficking roughly 4.9 million enslaved Africans—nearly 45% of the entire transatlantic slave trade—until Brazil became the last nation in the Americas to abolish slavery in 1888. Staying united after 1822 independence, Brazil expanded via the devastating War of the Triple Alliance and the 1903 Treaty of Petrópolis.

cards.name: Brunei
cards.story: Once a major Borneo maritime sultanate, Brunei was forcibly stripped of most of its territory in the 1800s as British adventurer James Brooke and the British North Borneo Company annexed Sarawak and Sabah—reducing Brunei to two tiny coastal enclaves. Placed under a British protectorate in 1888 and occupied by Japan during World War II, Brunei crushed an anti-colonial revolt in 1962 with British troops before regaining full independence in 1984.

cards.name: Bulgaria
cards.story: Bulgaria won autonomy after the 1877–78 Russo-Turkish War—amid massacres of both Bulgarian Christians and Ottoman Muslims that displaced hundreds of thousands—and full independence in 1908. Shifting borders through the Balkan Wars and World Wars settled in 1940; while Bulgaria saved ~48,000 Jews in its core territory during WWII, it deported over 11,300 Jews from occupied Thrace and Macedonia to Treblinka, and in 1989 its communist regime forcibly expelled ~350,000 ethnic Turks to Turkey.

cards.name: Burkina Faso
cards.story: France violently subjugated the Mossi kingdoms in the 1890s, imposing heavy forced labor—conscripting hundreds of thousands to build colonial railways and plantations in Côte d'Ivoire—while carving out, dismantling, and restoring Upper Volta's borders in 1947. Independent since 1960 and renamed Burkina Faso in 1984, recent Sahel insurgency conflicts since 2015 have killed over 20,000 people and displaced more than 2 million.

cards.name: Burundi
cards.story: Colonized first by Germany and then by Belgium after World War I, Burundi's centuries-old highland kingdom was subjected to colonial divide-and-rule policies that rigidified Hutu and Tutsi identities before independence in 1962. Post-independence mass violence—including the 1972 genocidal massacres of an estimated 100,000 to 200,000 Hutus and the 1993–2005 civil war that killed roughly 300,000 people—displaced over 1 million Burundians.

cards.name: Cambodia
cards.story: Heir to the medieval Khmer Empire, Cambodia was forced into a French colonial protectorate in 1863 before winning independence in 1953, only to be devastated by U.S. carpet bombing during the Vietnam War (1969–73) that killed an estimated 50,000 to 150,000 Cambodians and displaced up to 2 million. Between 1975 and 1979, the Khmer Rouge regime evacuated roughly 2 to 2.5 million city residents into forced labor camps and committed the Cambodian Genocide, killing an estimated 1.5 to 2 million people—roughly a quarter of the nation.

cards.name: Cameroon
cards.story: Germany seized Kamerun in 1884 using forced plantation labor before Britain and France partitioned it after World War I. To crush the UPC anti-colonial independence movement in the late 1950s and 1960s, French and allied forces waged a brutal counterinsurgency that killed tens of thousands of Cameroonians before French Cameroon (1960) and southern British Cameroons (1961) united; since 2017, conflict in the Anglophone regions has killed over 6,000 people and displaced more than 600,000.

cards.name: Canada
cards.story: Formed in 1867 when four British colonies united across Indigenous First Nations, Inuit, and Métis homelands, Canada expanded coast to coast through often-violated treaties, the military suppression of the 1885 North-West Resistance, and the displacement of Indigenous peoples onto reserves. Building on earlier 1830s colonial church boarding schools, Canada's federally funded residential school system (authorized in 1883 and operating until 1997)—characterized by the Truth and Reconciliation Commission as cultural genocide—forcibly removed ~150,000 Indigenous children from their families, with over 4,100 documented child deaths and estimates exceeding 6,000.

cards.name: Cape Verde
cards.story: Uninhabited until Portuguese colonizers arrived in the 1450s, Cabo Verde was built into a major transatlantic slave-trading hub where tens of thousands of enslaved Africans were held, sold, or forced onto plantations, and recurring colonial-era famines killed over 100,000 islanders between the 1700s and 1940s. Alongside Guinea-Bissau's liberation struggle and Portugal's 1974 revolution, Cabo Verde gained independence in 1975.

cards.name: Central African Republic
cards.story: France carved out Ubangi-Shari in the late 1800s and leased vast zones to private concession companies whose forced rubber and ivory collection, along with the Congo-Océan railway conscription, killed tens of thousands and sparked the 1928–31 Kongo-Wara rebellion. Independent since 1960 along arbitrary colonial lines, recurring civil wars since 2013 have killed tens of thousands and displaced over 1.2 million people—roughly a fifth of the population.

cards.name: Chad
cards.story: French military conquest around Lake Chad—including brutal pacification campaigns against the Ouaddai and Rabih az-Zubayr's realm in the 1890s–1910s—forced Saharan northern societies and southern farming communities into a single colonial territory. Independent since 1960, decades of civil war, border wars with Libya (resolved by the ICJ in 1994), and regional crises have killed tens of thousands and left Chad hosting over 1.2 million refugees from Sudan and neighboring states.

cards.name: Chile
cards.story: Winning independence from Spain in 1818, Chile expanded northward by defeating Peru and Bolivia in the War of the Pacific (1879–84) and expanded southward through the 1861–83 Occupation of Araucanía, which militarily subdued the autonomous Mapuche nation, confiscated over 90% of their ancestral land, and killed or displaced thousands. Later, Augusto Pinochet's 1973–90 U.S.-backed dictatorship killed or disappeared ~3,200 people, tortured ~38,000, and drove ~200,000 Chileans into exile.

cards.name: China
cards.story: China's modern borders inherit the multi-ethnic empire forged by Qing Dynasty conquests—including the 1750s Dzungar genocide in Xinjiang—before 19th-century Opium Wars and 'unequal treaties' ceded Hong Kong, Macau, and northern lands to foreign powers. The 1937–45 Japanese invasion killed an estimated 15 to 20 million Chinese people and displaced up to 95 million, followed by the Chinese Civil War (millions killed) establishing the PRC in 1949; subsequent state campaigns—including the Great Leap Forward famine (tens of millions dead), the 1959 Tibet crackdown (driving ~80,000+ Tibetans into exile), and mass detentions of Uyghurs in Xinjiang—deeply shaped modern control.
cards.contestedNote: China maintains active territorial disputes over self-governing Taiwan, Himalayan borders with India, and South China Sea maritime zones; UN experts have also cited severe human rights abuses and mass detentions in Xinjiang and repression in Tibet and Hong Kong.

cards.name: Colombia
cards.turningPoint: 1830–31 Dissolution of Gran Colombia & 1903 Panama Exit
cards.story: Spanish conquest devastated Muisca and other Indigenous societies and trafficked hundreds of thousands of enslaved Africans through Cartagena before Colombia led independence as Gran Colombia (as Venezuela and Ecuador seceded in 1830 prior to formal dissolution in 1831, before losing Panama in 1903). Modern Colombia has endured catastrophic internal violence: La Violencia (1948–58) killed ~200,000 people, and the multi-sided armed conflict since 1964 has killed over 450,000 people and internally displaced more than 8 million—one of the largest displacement crises in modern history.

cards.name: Comoros
cards.story: French colonial conquest in the 1800s absorbed the Indian Ocean sultanates of the Comoros, imposing plantation labor and reshaping island governance. When three of the four islands declared independence in 1975, France retained Mayotte despite UN General Assembly resolutions affirming Comorian territorial integrity—leaving a heavily policed maritime border where thousands of Comorian migrants have drowned trying to reach Mayotte.
cards.contestedNote: Comoros claims the fourth island of the archipelago, Mayotte, which France administers as an overseas department despite repeated UN General Assembly resolutions calling for its return.

cards.name: Costa Rica
cards.story: Spanish colonization in the 1500s decimated Costa Rica's Indigenous population by roughly 80–90% through epidemics, conquest, and forced labor before independence from Spain in 1821 and withdrawal from the Central American Federation in 1838. After a brief 1948 civil war that killed ~2,000 people, Costa Rica abolished its standing military and later absorbed hundreds of thousands of refugees fleeing wars in neighboring Nicaragua and El Salvador.

cards.name: Côte d'Ivoire
cards.story: France enforced colonial rule over Côte d'Ivoire in 1893 through military campaigns against Baule and other resisting kingdoms, imposing forced labor on cocoa and timber plantations and drawing arbitrary borders across ethnic homelands. Independent since 1960, post-independence political and identity conflicts—including civil wars in 2002–07 and 2010–11—killed several thousand people and displaced over 1 million.

cards.name: Croatia
cards.story: During World War II, Croatia's fascist Ustaše regime operated camps like Jasenovac, murdering roughly 300,000+ Serbs, ~30,000 Jews, and ~25,000 Roma. After declaring independence from Yugoslavia in 1991, the Croatian War of Independence (1991–95) killed ~20,000 people—including early Serbian ethnic cleansing of ~200,000+ Croats and Croatia's 1995 Operation Storm, which expelled roughly 150,000–200,000 ethnic Serbs—locking in Croatia's modern borders.

cards.name: Cuba
cards.story: Spanish conquest in 1511 nearly wiped out Cuba's Indigenous Taíno and Ciboney peoples through massacres, forced labor, and disease, after which Spain trafficked roughly 780,000 to 800,000 enslaved Africans to work sugar plantations until abolishing slavery only in 1886. During Cuba's 1895–98 War of Independence, Spanish 'reconcentration' camps killed an estimated 150,000 to 200,000 Cuban civilians before U.S. military intervention ended Spanish rule in 1898 and left the U.S. holding Guantánamo Bay.

cards.name: Cyprus
cards.story: Cyprus won independence from Britain in 1960 after an anti-colonial insurgency and communal tensions between Greek and Turkish Cypriots. In 1974, a Greek-junta-backed coup triggered a Turkish military invasion that occupied the northern 37% of the island, killed several thousand people, and forcibly displaced roughly 200,000 Cypriots (~160,000–170,000 Greek Cypriots south and ~45,000–50,000 Turkish Cypriots north) across the UN Green Line.
cards.contestedNote: The Republic of Cyprus is internationally recognized across the whole island, while Turkey militarily occupies the northern third (self-declared Northern Cyprus, recognized only by Turkey) since the 1974 invasion that displaced ~200,000 people.

cards.name: Czech Republic
cards.story: After Austria-Hungary collapsed in 1918, Czechs and Slovaks formed Czechoslovakia—which Nazi Germany dismembered in 1938–39, murdering roughly 260,000–270,000 Czechoslovak Jews and thousands of Roma during the Holocaust. Following WWII, Czechoslovakia expelled roughly 2.5 to 3 million ethnic Sudeten Germans (with ~15,000–30,000 deaths) and endured the 1968 Soviet-led invasion before peacefully splitting from Slovakia in 1993.

cards.name: Denmark
cards.story: One of Europe's oldest kingdoms, Denmark lost Norway (1814) and Schleswig-Holstein to Prussia (1864) before a 1920 plebiscite fixed its southern border with Germany—and during Nazi occupation (1940–45), Danes famously evacuated ~7,200 Jews to Sweden. Globally, Denmark also operated colonial outposts in West Africa and the Caribbean (trafficking ~100,000 enslaved Africans) and imposed forced assimilation policies in colonial Greenland, including non-consensual birth control on thousands of Inuit women.

cards.name: Djibouti
cards.story: France seized strategic coastal lands at the Red Sea entrance in the late 1800s as French Somaliland, dividing Afar and Somali communities across colonial boundaries with Ethiopia, Eritrea, and Somalia. Following decades of colonial repression—including the 1967 crackdown on pro-independence demonstrators—Djibouti won independence in 1977, though a 1991–94 civil war displaced tens of thousands.

cards.name: Dominica
cards.story: Indigenous Kalinago warriors fiercely defended mountainous Dominica for over two centuries against European invasion—even after French and British colonizers massacred Kalinago communities on neighboring islands—before Britain seized control in 1763, restricting survivors to a small coastal tract before formally establishing the 3,700-acre Carib Reserve (Kalinago Territory) in 1903 while importing ~100,000 enslaved Africans for plantations. Dominica gained independence as a republic in 1978.

cards.name: Dominican Republic
cards.story: After Spanish colonization in 1492 devastated Hispaniola's Indigenous Taíno population (from hundreds of thousands to near extinction within decades) and introduced African plantation slavery, colonial treaties split the island between French Haiti and Spanish Santo Domingo. Following 22 years of unified Haitian rule, the eastern two-thirds declared independence in 1844; in 1937, dictator Rafael Trujillo's army carried out the Parsley Massacre along the border, murdering an estimated 15,000 to 20,000 ethnic Haitians.

cards.name: DR Congo
cards.story: At the 1885 Berlin Conference, European powers handed the Congo basin to Belgium's King Leopold II as his personal colony; forced rubber extraction, mutilations, executions, and induced famine and disease caused an estimated 1.5 to 10 million population loss among Congolese people before Belgium took direct colonial control in 1908. After winning independence in 1960—followed by the foreign-backed assassination of Patrice Lumumba—the First and Second Congo Wars (1996–2003) and ongoing eastern conflicts have caused an estimated 5.4 million excess deaths and displaced over 7 million people.

cards.name: East Timor
cards.story: Colonial treaties split Timor between Dutch west and Portuguese east. Days after East Timor declared independence in 1975, Indonesia invaded and occupied the territory for 24 years with Western diplomatic backing; the CAVR truth commission and demographers estimate 102,800 to 200,000 East Timorese died from killings, forced resettlement, and engineered starvation (roughly a quarter of the population), and pro-Indonesia militias displaced another 240,000 after voters chose independence in 1999—leading to Timor-Leste's sovereignty in 2002.

cards.name: Ecuador
cards.story: Spanish conquest in the 1530s crushed the northern Inca Empire and imposed forced encomienda and mita labor on Indigenous peoples before Ecuador left Gran Colombia in 1830 and claimed the Galápagos in 1832. Border wars with Peru—notably the 1941 war, in which Peru seized roughly 40% of Ecuador's claimed Amazonian territory, and the 1995 Cenepa War—killed hundreds and displaced tens of thousands before a 1998 peace treaty fixed the border.

cards.name: Egypt
cards.story: Anchored by the Nile for over five millennia, Egypt was subjected to British military occupation starting in 1882 while Ottoman and British colonial treaties drew its straight desert borders across Nubian and Bedouin homelands—later flooding ancestral Nubian villages and displacing roughly 100,000 Nubians during the Aswan High Dam project. Wars with Israel in 1956, 1967, and 1973 killed tens of thousands before Egypt regained the Sinai Peninsula under the 1979 peace treaty.

cards.name: El Salvador
cards.story: Spanish conquest in the 1520s subjugated Pipil and Lenca societies before El Salvador broke from Spain (1821) and the Central American Federation (1841). In 1932, the military regime carried out La Matanza—massacring an estimated 10,000 to 30,000 mostly Indigenous peasants—and the U.S.-backed 1980–92 civil war killed roughly 75,000 Salvadorans (including massacres like El Mozote) and displaced over 1 million people.

cards.name: Equatorial Guinea
cards.story: Portugal traded the Gulf of Guinea island of Bioko and mainland coastal claims to Spain in 1778, where Spanish colonial plantations relied heavily on coerced and indentured African labor while devastating the Indigenous Bubi population. Following independence in 1968, Francisco Macías Nguema's dictatorship killed tens of thousands and drove roughly a third of the entire population—over 100,000 people—into exile; in January 2026, the government formally relocated the national capital from Malabo on Bioko Island to the newly built mainland city of Ciudad de la Paz.

cards.name: Eritrea
cards.story: Italy seized Eritrea's Red Sea coast as a colony in 1890 before post-WWII decisions federated it with—and Ethiopia forcibly annexed it in 1962—triggering a 30-year war of independence that killed an estimated 150,000 to 250,000 combatants and civilians and displaced hundreds of thousands. Eritreans voted overwhelmingly for independence in 1993, though a 1998–2000 border war with Ethiopia killed roughly 70,000–100,000 more and displaced over 1 million across both nations.

cards.name: Estonia
cards.story: Estonia won independence from imperial Russia in 1918–20 before the Soviet Union forcibly annexed it in 1940, followed by Nazi German occupation (1941–44) and renewed Soviet rule until 1991. Combined WWII fighting, the Holocaust, and Soviet mass deportations of 1941 and 1949 sent over 30,000 Estonians to Siberian gulags and drove ~70,000–80,000 into exile—reducing Estonia's population by roughly one-fifth before the 1991 Singing Revolution restored sovereignty.

cards.name: Eswatini
cards.story: Consolidating the Swazi Kingdom in the 1800s, Swazi rulers saw much of their ancestral grazing land seized through coercive settler concessions and British-Boer treaties before Britain declared a protectorate in 1903, leaving large ethnic Swazi communities inside South Africa. Independent since 1968 and renamed Eswatini in 2018, its borders still reflect those colonial land losses.

cards.name: Ethiopia
cards.story: Ethiopia defeated Italy's colonial invasion at Adwa in 1896, though Fascist Italy's brutal 1935–41 occupation—using poison gas and massacres such as Yekatit 12—killed an estimated 300,000 to 750,000 Ethiopians. Decades of civil wars, Eritrean secession in 1993, and the 2020–22 Tigray War—which caused an estimated 300,000 to 600,000 conflict and famine deaths and displaced over 2 million people—have deeply scarred its modern state.

cards.name: Fiji
cards.story: After decades of colonial pressure and musket warfare led Fijian chiefs to cede sovereignty to Britain in 1874, a British-introduced 1875 measles epidemic killed roughly 40,000 Indigenous Fijians—about a third of the population. To staff colonial sugar plantations, Britain brought over 60,000 Indian girmitiya indentured laborers under harsh contracts between 1879 and 1916; Fiji gained independence in 1970.

cards.name: Finland
cards.story: After centuries under Swedish and Russian rule, Finland declared independence in 1917—immediately enduring a bitter 1918 civil war that killed ~37,000 people. During World War II's Winter War and Continuation War against the USSR (killing ~95,000 Finns), peace treaties forced Finland to cede Karelia and Petsamo to the Soviet Union, permanently uprooting roughly 420,000 Karelian Finns (over 11% of Finland's population) from their homes.

cards.name: France
cards.story: France's European borders solidified through royal conquests, wars with Germany, and minor 1947 Paris Peace Treaty Alpine adjustments with Italy—World War I alone killed ~1.4 million French soldiers, and during WWII Vichy France collaborated in deporting ~76,000 Jews to Nazi death camps. Globally, France built a vast colonial empire across Africa, Asia, and the Caribbean, trafficking over 1.3 million enslaved Africans, killing hundreds of thousands in Algeria, Indochina, and Madagascar, and retaining overseas territories today.

cards.name: French Guiana
cards.story: France colonized Guiana in the 1600s, decimating Indigenous Kalina and Teko populations, trafficking enslaved Africans onto coastal plantations, and operating the notorious Devil's Island penal colony (1852–1953) where roughly 50,000 of ~70,000 deported convicts died from disease and brutal labor. In 1946 it became an overseas department of France and part of the European Union.
cards.contestedNote: French Guiana is not a sovereign country, but a full overseas region of France governed under French and EU law.

cards.name: Gabon
cards.story: France imposed coastal treaties in the 1840s and expanded through military expeditions into Gabon's rainforest interior as part of French Equatorial Africa, using forced timber and rubber concessions that depopulated rural villages through labor abuse and famine. Gabon became independent along those colonial borders in 1960.

cards.name: Gambia
cards.story: The Gambia's narrow, winding border was carved out solely by an 1889 imperial bargain between Britain and France—giving Britain roughly six miles on either side of the Gambia River and splitting Mandinka, Wolof, and Fula families across Senegal. Before colonial partitioning, British and European traders also trafficked hundreds of thousands of enslaved Africans from the Senegambia river ports; Gambia won independence in 1965.

cards.name: Georgia
cards.story: Annexed by the Russian Empire in the 1800s and invaded by the Soviet Red Army in 1921 after three years of independence, Georgia endured Stalin-era purges and WWII losses before restoring independence in 1991. Separatist wars in Abkhazia and South Ossetia (1991–93) and Russia's 2008 invasion killed thousands and forcibly displaced roughly 250,000 to 300,000 ethnic Georgians from both regions.
cards.contestedNote: Abkhazia and South Ossetia are internationally recognized as part of Georgia, though both operate as Russian-occupied breakaway regions from which ~250,000+ ethnic Georgians were ethnically cleansed and remain displaced.

cards.name: Germany
cards.story: Unified through Bismarck's wars in 1871, Imperial Germany committed the 1904–08 Herero and Nama genocide in Namibia (~75,000–90,000 killed) and fought World War I (~2 million German military dead). Under Nazi rule (1933–45), Germany launched World War II—causing over 60 million deaths worldwide—and orchestrated the Holocaust, murdering 6 million European Jews alongside millions of Soviet POWs, Poles, Roma, and disabled people; post-war defeat split Germany until 1990, shifted its eastern border west to the Oder-Neisse line, and led to the expulsion of 12 to 14 million ethnic Germans (500,000–600,000 dead).

cards.name: Ghana
cards.story: Britain fought multiple Anglo-Ashanti Wars across the 1800s—burning Kumasi in 1874 and exiling King Prempeh I—to force the Ashanti Kingdom, northern territories, and coastal Gold Coast into one colony, whose coast had previously seen over 1 million enslaved Africans trafficked through forts like Cape Coast and Elmina. Combined with a strip of Togoland, Ghana became the first Black-majority European colony in sub-Saharan West Africa to win independence in 1957 (following Sudan's 1956 independence from Anglo-Egyptian rule).

cards.name: Greece
cards.story: Greece won independence from the Ottoman Empire in 1830 after a bloody nine-year war that killed tens of thousands of Greeks and Muslims, then expanded through the Balkan Wars and World Wars (adding the Dodecanese in 1947). In 1922–23, after the Smyrna catastrophe and Ottoman genocides, the compulsory Greece–Turkey population exchange forcibly uprooted ~1.2 million Greek Orthodox Christians from Anatolia to Greece and ~350,000–400,000 Muslims to Turkey; Nazi WWII occupation later killed ~300,000 Greeks through famine and murdered ~60,000 Greek Jews.

cards.name: Grenada
cards.story: After French colonizers invaded Grenada in 1649–51—driving Indigenous Kalinago defenders to mass deaths at Leapers' Hill—and Britain seized the island in 1763, colonizers trafficked over 130,000 enslaved Africans onto its spice and sugar plantations and crushed Fédon's 1795–96 anti-slavery rebellion, killing thousands. Independent from Britain since 1974, Grenada later endured a 1983 coup and U.S. military invasion.

cards.name: Guatemala
cards.story: Once the heart of Maya civilization, Guatemala was conquered by Spain in 1524 through wars, forced labor, and epidemics that killed an estimated 80–90% of the Indigenous population before independence in 1821. During the 1960–96 Guatemalan Civil War—following a 1954 U.S.-backed coup—a UN truth commission concluded state forces committed genocide against the Maya people, killing or disappearing over 200,000 people (~83% Indigenous Maya), razing hundreds of villages, and displacing over 1 million.

cards.name: Guinea
cards.story: France conquered Guinea in the 1880s–90s by crushing resistance led by Samori Touré's Wassoulou Empire and the Futa Jallon Imamate, folding the region into French West Africa with forced labor and taxation. Guinea boldly voted 'No' to France's colonial community in 1958, prompting France to strip public infrastructure overnight as Guinea became independent; later repression under Sékou Touré killed thousands and forced over 1 million Guineans into exile.

cards.name: Guinea-Bissau
cards.story: Carved out by an 1886 colonial bargain between Portugal and France after centuries of Portuguese slave trading along its rivers, Portuguese Guinea endured brutal colonial extraction until Amílcar Cabral's PAIGC launched an 11-year armed liberation war (1963–74) that killed an estimated 15,000 people and displaced over 150,000 before Portugal recognized Guinea-Bissau's independence in 1974.

cards.name: Guyana
cards.story: Dutch and later British colonizers (from 1814) built British Guiana's sugar economy on hundreds of thousands of enslaved Africans—brutally crushing the 1763 Berbice and 1823 Demerara slave uprisings—followed by nearly 240,000 Indian indentured laborers after emancipation. Guyana won independence in 1966, though Venezuela continues to claim the oil-rich western Essequibo region.
cards.contestedNote: Guyana administers the Essequibo region (~two-thirds of its territory) under an 1899 arbitration award, which Venezuela disputes.

cards.name: Haiti
cards.story: Spanish colonization nearly annihilated Hispaniola's Indigenous Taíno people before France turned western Saint-Domingue into the world's deadliest sugar colony, trafficking roughly 770,000 to 860,000 enslaved Africans. In the 1791–1804 Haitian Revolution—killing an estimated 200,000–350,000 Haitians and tens of thousands of French troops—formerly enslaved people overthrew slavery and colonial rule to found the world's first independent Black republic, though France later extorted a crippling 'independence debt' at gunpoint in 1825.

cards.name: Honduras
cards.story: Spanish conquest in the 1520s–30s devastated Lenca and Maya populations through slaving raids, forced mining, and disease before Honduras left Spain (1821) and the Central American Federation (1838), later absorbing the formerly British-controlled Bay Islands and Miskito Coast. In the 1980s, Honduras served as a U.S.-backed staging ground for regional Cold War conflicts while domestic death squads disappeared hundreds and tens of thousands of Central American refugees crossed its borders.

cards.name: Hungary
cards.story: Following Austria-Hungary's defeat in World War I, the 1920 Treaty of Trianon stripped Hungary of roughly two-thirds of its former kingdom's territory, leaving ~3.3 million ethnic Hungarians outside its new borders and triggering ~350,000–400,000 refugees. During World War II, Hungarian authorities collaborated with Nazi Germany in the 1944 deportation and murder of roughly 565,000 Hungarian Jews; Soviet tanks later crushed the 1956 Hungarian Revolution, killing ~2,500–3,000 and driving ~200,000 into exile.

cards.name: Iceland
cards.story: Settled by Norse and Celtic voyagers over a thousand years ago—including enslaved Gaelic captives brought from Ireland and Britain—Iceland spent centuries under Norwegian and Danish colonial trade monopolies. When Nazi Germany occupied Denmark during World War II, Allied forces occupied Iceland, and Icelanders voted overwhelmingly in 1944 to become a fully independent republic.

cards.name: India
cards.story: After nearly two centuries of British colonial extraction—marked by colonial-era famines such as the 1943 Bengal Famine that killed an estimated 2 to 3 million people—Britain hastily partitioned British India in August 1947 into India and Pakistan. Partition unleashed catastrophic communal massacres that killed an estimated 500,000 to 2 million people and displaced 12 to 18 million across Punjab and Bengal, while over 560 princely states were integrated—some by military force, as in Hyderabad and contested Kashmir.
cards.contestedNote: India's northern borders remain heavily militarized due to unresolved disputes with Pakistan over Kashmir—where insurgency and military crackdowns since 1989 have killed tens of thousands and displaced hundreds of thousands—and with China along the Line of Actual Control.

cards.name: Indonesia
cards.story: After more than three centuries of Dutch colonial rule—including the Aceh War (1873–1914) that killed an estimated 60,000–100,000 Acehnese—Indonesia declared independence in 1945 and fought a four-year war against Dutch reoccupation (killing roughly 100,000 Indonesians) before winning recognition in 1949. In 1965–66, military-backed anti-communist purges killed an estimated 500,000 to 1 million people and imprisoned over 1 million; Indonesia's disputed 1969 annexation of West Papua also triggered a long-running conflict killing tens of thousands of Indigenous Papuans.
cards.contestedNote: West Papua was incorporated into Indonesia via a heavily coerced 1969 vote (the 'Act of Free Choice'); Indigenous Papuan independence movements continue to report military repression, killings, and internal displacement.

cards.name: Iran
cards.story: Inheriting millennia of Persian statehood, Iran was never formally colonized, yet 19th-century wars and treaties with Russia and Britain stripped away its Caucasus and Central Asian territories (with later 1932 Turkish frontier treaties and the 1975 Algiers Agreement with Iraq finalizing its western borders) while foreign occupation during both World Wars triggered devastating famines killing hundreds of thousands. Following the 1979 Revolution, the 1980–88 Iran–Iraq War killed an estimated 500,000 to 1 million people across both nations and displaced over 1 million Iranians from border provinces.

cards.name: Iraq
cards.story: After the Ottoman Empire's defeat in World War I, Britain forcibly merged three distinct provinces—Mosul, Baghdad, and Basra—into one mandate, crushing the 1920 Iraqi Revolt with aerial bombing that killed thousands before granting formal independence in 1932. Saddam Hussein's regime committed the 1988 Anfal genocide against Iraqi Kurds—murdering an estimated 50,000 to 100,000 (up to 180,000 in Kurdish counts), razing ~4,000 villages, and displacing ~1 million—followed by the 2003 U.S.-led invasion, sectarian civil war, and ISIS conflict (including the 2014 Yazidi genocide), causing hundreds of thousands of deaths and displacing over 6 million Iraqis.

cards.name: Ireland
cards.story: Subjected to centuries of English and British conquest, land confiscations, and colonial plantations—including Oliver Cromwell's brutal 1649–53 campaign and the 1845–52 Great Famine, during which ~1 million Irish people starved to death and ~1 to 2 million emigrated under British laissez-faire rule—Ireland fought the 1919–21 War of Independence. The 1921 Anglo-Irish Treaty partitioned the island into 26 southern counties and British-ruled Northern Ireland, where the 1968–98 Troubles later killed over 3,500 people.

cards.name: Israel
cards.story: Shaped by modern Zionism—a political movement developed largely in Europe and the United States, about which Jewish communities worldwide hold diverse and opposing viewpoints—Israel declared independence in May 1948 following the British Mandate of Palestine and the 1947 UN Partition Plan. Its establishment was accompanied by the Nakba, the mass displacement of over 700,000 Palestinians from their homes. The 1949 armistice lines ('Green Line') set its initial boundaries, and the 1967 war brought the West Bank, East Jerusalem, Gaza, and the Golan Heights under Israeli military occupation.
cards.contestedNote: Israel's borders with Palestine, Jerusalem's status, and the Golan Heights remain internationally disputed. Continued Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank—illegal under international law—alongside continued ethnic cleansing, displacement, and actions in Gaza widely described by UN experts and human rights organizations as genocide (killing over 70,000 Palestinians and displacing the vast majority of Gaza's 2.2 million residents since 2023) remain central to the ongoing conflict.

cards.name: Italy
cards.story: Unified through the 1861 Risorgimento wars and adjusted along the Alps and Adriatic after both World Wars—which forced ~250,000–350,000 ethnic Italians to flee Istria and Dalmatia after 1945—Italy also waged brutal colonial conquests under Fascism. Italian forces killed 50,000–70,000 Libyans in desert concentration camps (1929–34) and 300,000–750,000 Ethiopians (1935–41) using poison gas and massacres, while collaborating in the WWII deportation of ~7,500–8,000 Italian Jews.

cards.name: Jamaica
cards.story: Spain colonized Jamaica in 1509, wiping out most of the Indigenous Taíno population before Britain seized the island in 1655 and turned it into a massive slave-sugar colony that imported over 1 million enslaved Africans. Escaped African Maroon communities fought fierce guerrilla wars against British armies, and Britain brutally crushed the 1831 Baptist War and 1865 Morant Bay Rebellion (killing hundreds) before Jamaica won independence in 1962.

cards.name: Japan
cards.turningPoint: 1951 San Francisco Treaty & 1972 Return of Okinawa
cards.story: After annexing Indigenous Ainu lands in Hokkaido and the Ryukyu Kingdom (Okinawa) in the late 1800s, Imperial Japan conquered Taiwan, Korea, Manchuria, and much of East and Southeast Asia—inflicting mass atrocities including the Nanjing Massacre and forced labor that contributed to roughly 15 to 20+ million Asian civilian deaths during World War II. Japan itself suffered roughly 2.5 to 3.1 million wartime deaths, including the firebombing of its cities, the Battle of Okinawa (over 100,000 Okinawan civilians killed), and the U.S. atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki (~150,000–246,000 killed), before the U.S. returned Okinawa in 1972.
cards.contestedNote: Japan and Russia still dispute four northern islands (the Southern Kurils / Northern Territories) seized by the USSR in 1945, from which ~17,000 Japanese residents were expelled.

cards.name: Jordan
cards.story: Britain carved Transjordan east of the Jordan River from former Ottoman Syria in 1921 before recognizing its independence in 1946. Regional wars reshaped its population profoundly: Jordan absorbed hundreds of thousands of Palestinian refugees displaced by the 1948 Nakba and 1967 Israeli occupation of the West Bank (today over 2 million registered Palestinian refugees live in Jordan), alongside over 600,000 Syrian refugees since 2011.

cards.name: Kazakhstan
cards.story: Spanning the Eurasian steppe of the Kazakh khanates, Kazakhstan was conquered by the Russian Empire in the 18th–19th centuries and subjected to Soviet forced collectivization and nomadic sedentarization. During the 1930–33 Kazakh Famine (Asharshylyk), an estimated 1.3 to 1.5 million ethnic Kazakhs—roughly 38% to 42% of the entire Kazakh people—starved to death while over 665,000 to 1 million fled as refugees, and Stalin later deported over 1 million Chechens, Koreans, Poles, and Volga Germans into Kazakhstan before independence in 1991.

cards.name: Kenya
cards.story: Britain and Germany partitioned East Africa across Indigenous homelands in 1886, and British settlers seized millions of acres of fertile highland land from Kikuyu, Maasai, and Kalenjin communities. During the 1952–60 Mau Mau anticolonial uprising, Britain detained up to 150,000 Kenyans in brutal camps and fenced 'emergency villages' holding over 1 million people—with demographic studies estimating 15,000 to 50,000 excess African deaths—before Kenya won independence in 1963.

cards.name: Kiribati
cards.story: Britain imposed colonial rule over the Gilbert Islands in 1892 and phosphate-rich Banaba (Ocean Island), where British strip-mining devastated the island—leading colonial authorities to forcibly relocate the entire Banaban population (~1,000 people) to Rabi Island in Fiji after World War II's brutal Japanese occupation and Battle of Tarawa (~6,000 dead). After the Ellice Islands split away as Tuvalu, Kiribati gained independence in 1979.

cards.name: Kosovo
cards.story: After Serbia stripped Kosovo's autonomy within Yugoslavia in 1989, the 1998–99 Kosovo War saw Serbian and Yugoslav forces kill over 10,000 Kosovar Albanians and conduct mass ethnic cleansing that forcibly expelled roughly 850,000–900,000 Albanians across borders (over half the population) before NATO airstrikes forced a withdrawal—followed by retaliatory expulsions of over 100,000 Kosovo Serbs and Roma. Administered by the UN, Kosovo declared independence in 2008.
cards.contestedNote: Kosovo declared independence in 2008 after the 1998–99 war and ethnic cleansing; over 100 countries recognize its statehood, while Serbia and several other nations do not.

cards.name: Kuwait
cards.story: Founded as a Gulf trading town in the 1700s, Kuwait accepted British colonial protection in 1899, and a 1922 British-imposed border treaty fixed its desert lines with Iraq and Saudi Arabia before independence in 1961. In August 1990, Iraq invaded and occupied Kuwait for seven months—killing over 1,000 Kuwaitis, displacing roughly 400,000 residents, and torching hundreds of oil wells—before a U.S.-led coalition expelled Iraqi forces in the 1991 Gulf War (which also led to the expulsion of ~300,000–400,000 Palestinian residents from Kuwait).

cards.name: Kyrgyzstan
cards.story: Conquered by the Russian Empire in the 1800s, Kyrgyz communities rose against imperial conscription and settler land seizures in the 1916 Central Asian Revolt (Urkun), which Russian troops crushed with massacres and forced flight across the Tian Shan mountains into China that killed an estimated 100,000 to 270,000 Kyrgyz and Kazakhs. Soviet boundary planners drew Kyrgyzstan's republic borders in the 1920s–30s; independent since 1991, ethnic clashes in southern Osh in 2010 killed hundreds and displaced ~400,000.

cards.name: Laos
cards.story: Tracing its roots to the Kingdom of Lan Xang, Laos's Mekong borders were fixed in 1893 when France forced Siam to cede eastern territories into French Indochina before independence in 1953. During the Vietnam War's 'Secret War' (1964–73), the United States dropped over 2 million tons of bombs on Laos—making it the most heavily bombed country per capita in history—killing an estimated 50,000 to 200,000 Laotians, displacing roughly 700,000 (a quarter of the population), and forcing over 300,000 refugees (including many Hmong) abroad.

cards.name: Latvia
cards.story: Latvia won independence from imperial Russia in 1918–20 before the Soviet Union forcibly annexed it in 1940, followed by Nazi German occupation (1941–44) and renewed Soviet rule. During WWII, Nazi forces and local collaborators murdered roughly 70,000 Latvian Jews (~90% of the Jewish population), while Soviet deportations in 1941 and 1949 sent over 57,000 Latvians to Siberian gulags and ~150,000+ fled into exile before independence was restored in 1991.

cards.name: Lebanon
cards.story: After the Ottoman Empire collapsed—following the 1915–18 Great Famine of Mount Lebanon that killed an estimated 150,000 to 200,000 people—France carved Greater Lebanon out of Syria in 1920 before independence in 1943. Confessional divisions, regional wars, Israeli invasions/occupations (1978–2000 and 2024), and the 1975–90 Lebanese Civil War killed roughly 120,000 to 150,000 people and displaced nearly 1 million; Lebanon also shelters over 1 million Palestinian and Syrian refugees.

cards.name: Lesotho
cards.story: Founded by King Moshoeshoe I in the 1820s as a mountain sanctuary during the devastating Mfecane regional upheavals, the Basotho kingdom lost much of its fertile western lowlands in wars with Boer settlers before seeking British protection in 1868 to avoid complete annexation. Entirely surrounded by South Africa, Lesotho gained independence in 1966 along those shrunken borders.

cards.name: Liberia
cards.story: Established in the 1820s by the American Colonization Society for freed African Americans—whose settler elite marginalized and fought Indigenous coastal and interior peoples—Liberia declared independence in 1847 while British and French colonial empires later stripped away parts of its frontier. Two devastating civil wars between 1989 and 2003 killed an estimated 250,000 people and displaced over 1 million—nearly a third of the country.

cards.name: Libya
cards.story: Italy invaded Ottoman Libya in 1911 and waged a ruthless two-decade war to crush Senussi resistance: between 1929 and 1934, Fascist Italy forcibly marched roughly 100,000 Cyrenaican Bedouin civilians into desert concentration camps where an estimated 50,000 to 70,000 died from execution, starvation, and disease before Italy united three provinces into Libya in 1934. Independent in 1951 after Italy's WWII defeat, post-2011 civil conflicts have killed tens of thousands and displaced hundreds of thousands.

cards.name: Liechtenstein
cards.turningPoint: 1806 End of the Holy Roman Empire
cards.story: Formed when the Liechtenstein family united two small Alpine estates in 1719, this microstate gained full sovereignty when Napoleon dissolved the Holy Roman Empire in 1806. Neutrality and close economic ties with Switzerland have kept its borders unchanged for over two centuries.

cards.name: Lithuania
cards.story: Once part of a vast medieval Grand Duchy, Lithuania won independence in 1918 before Poland seized Vilnius (1920) and the USSR forcibly annexed the country in 1940 (returning Vilnius). During Nazi occupation (1941–44), Germans and local collaborators murdered roughly 195,000 to 200,000 Lithuanian Jews (~90–95% of its Jewish community), while Soviet deportations and post-war anti-Soviet partisan warfare (1944–53) killed over 20,000 and deported ~130,000 to Siberia before Lithuania led the break from the USSR in 1990.

cards.name: Luxembourg
cards.story: Carved out by the 1839 Treaty of London—which transferred its larger French-speaking western half to Belgium—Luxembourg had its neutrality guaranteed in 1867. Despite neutrality, Germany invaded and occupied Luxembourg in both World Wars, forcibly conscripting over 10,000 Luxembourgers into the Wehrmacht and murdering ~1,300 to 2,000 Jews from its small Jewish population during the Holocaust.

cards.name: Madagascar
cards.story: Unified largely under the Merina Kingdom, Madagascar was invaded and annexed by France in 1895–96 after a war that killed thousands and abolished the monarchy. When Malagasy nationalists rose up against French colonial rule in 1947–48, French forces crushed the rebellion through mass executions, village burnings, and induced famine that killed an estimated 30,000 to 100,000 people before independence arrived in 1960.

cards.name: Malawi
cards.story: Devastated in the 19th century by the East African slave trade, the Lake Malawi basin was claimed by Britain as Nyasaland in 1891 via imperial treaties with Portugal, imposing harsh colonial hut taxes and plantation labor that sparked John Chilembwe's 1915 uprising. After resisting a white-minority colonial federation—during which British forces killed dozens in the 1959 State of Emergency—Malawi won independence in 1964.

cards.name: Malaysia
cards.story: Britain consolidated colonial control over Malaya and northern Borneo through treaties and military interventions, building tin and rubber economies on mass Chinese and Indian labor migration; Japan's 1941–45 occupation killed tens of thousands, followed by the 1948–60 Malayan Emergency counterinsurgency in which Britain forcibly relocated ~500,000 mostly ethnic Chinese civilians into fenced 'New Villages' and killed ~11,000. Malaya (1957) joined Sabah, Sarawak, and Singapore in 1963 before Singapore's 1965 separation.

cards.name: Maldives
cards.story: Comprising roughly 1,200 Indian Ocean coral islands, the Maldives resisted a brutal 15-year Portuguese colonial occupation (1558–73) before entering a British protectorate treaty in 1887 that gave Britain control of its foreign policy and strategic southern airbases. The archipelago regained full independence from Britain in 1965.

cards.name: Mali
cards.story: Home to the medieval empires of Ghana, Mali, and Songhai, the region was invaded and conquered by France in the late 1800s as French Sudan, crushing local resistance and imposing forced labor while splitting Tuareg and other nomadic peoples across colonial borders. Independent since 1960, rebellions and Sahel conflicts since 2012 have killed over 15,000 people and displaced hundreds of thousands.

cards.name: Malta
cards.story: Positioned at a strategic Mediterranean choke point, Malta was ruled successively by Phoenicians, the Knights of St. John, Napoleon's France, and the British Empire from 1800 onward. During World War II, relentless Axis aerial bombardments made Malta one of the most heavily bombed places on Earth, killing over 1,500 civilians and destroying thousands of buildings before Malta gained independence from Britain in 1964.

cards.name: Marshall Islands
cards.story: Passed from German and Japanese colonial rule into a U.S.-run UN Trust Territory after fierce World War II battles at Kwajalein and Enewetak (~10,000+ combatant deaths), the Marshall Islands endured 67 U.S. nuclear weapons tests between 1946 and 1958—including the 1954 Castle Bravo thermonuclear blast. The tests contaminated atolls with radioactive fallout, caused generational radiation illnesses, and forcibly displaced islanders from Bikini, Enewetak, Rongelap, and Utrik before independence in 1986.

cards.name: Mauritania
cards.story: France militarily conquered Saharan emirates in the early 1900s and drew geometric desert borders combining Arab-Berber and Black West African communities into Mauritania before independence in 1960. Border tensions and ethnic violence with Senegal in 1989–91 led Mauritania's regime to kill hundreds and forcibly expel roughly 60,000 to 75,000 Black Mauritanians across the Senegal River.

cards.name: Mauritius
cards.story: Uninhabited before European colonization, Dutch, French, and British empires built Mauritius's sugar economy on hundreds of thousands of enslaved Africans and, after abolition, over 450,000 Indian indentured laborers. Before granting independence in 1968, Britain unlawfully detached the Chagos Islands and forcibly expelled the entire Indigenous Chagossian population—roughly 1,500 to 2,000 people—to build a U.S.–UK military base on Diego Garcia.
cards.contestedNote: Britain forcibly expelled roughly 1,500–2,000 Chagossians between 1968 and 1973 after detaching the Chagos Archipelago from Mauritius; following a 2019 ICJ advisory opinion, the UK and Mauritius signed a May 2025 sovereignty transfer treaty, though as of late 2026 UK ratification remains stalled and Chagossian right-of-return disputes persist.

cards.name: Mexico
cards.story: Spain's 1519–21 conquest of the Aztec Empire and subsequent colonial rule triggered a catastrophic collapse of Mexico's Indigenous population—dropping from roughly 15–25 million to ~1–2 million within a century from epidemics, warfare, and forced labor. After winning independence in 1821, Mexico lost roughly half its national territory to the United States through Texas's secession and the 1846–48 U.S.–Mexico War, and later suffered 1 to 2 million deaths during the 1910–20 Mexican Revolution.

cards.name: Micronesia
cards.story: Colonized successively by Spain (whose 1887–90 wars crushed Pohnpeian resistance), Germany (which killed and exiled hundreds in the 1910–11 Sokehs Rebellion), and Japan—whose World War II militarization and U.S. bombardments at Chuuk Lagoon killed thousands of soldiers and Micronesians—the islands passed to a U.S.-run UN Trust Territory before four island states united as independent Micronesia in 1986.

cards.name: Moldova
cards.story: Carved out in 1940 when the Soviet Union seized Bessarabia from Romania—followed by Stalinist deportations of over 60,000 Moldovans to Siberia and the WWII Romanian-Nazi Holocaust murdering an estimated 200,000 to 300,000 Jews across Bessarabia, Bukovina, and Transnistria—Moldova became independent in 1991. A 1992 war over the Russian-backed breakaway region of Transnistria killed ~1,000 people and displaced over 100,000.
cards.contestedNote: The eastern strip of Transnistria has operated as a Russian-backed breakaway territory since the 1992 conflict (~1,000 killed, ~100,000+ displaced), though it remains internationally recognized as part of Moldova.

cards.name: Monaco
cards.story: Ruled by the Grimaldi dynasty since 1297, Monaco surrendered the neighboring Riviera towns of Menton and Roquebrune to France in the 1861 treaty in exchange for formal French recognition of its compact coastal borders. During World War II, Axis occupation resulted in the arrest and deportation of roughly 90 Jews from Monaco to Nazi death camps.

cards.name: Mongolia
cards.story: Once the core of the 13th-century Mongol Empire, Outer Mongolia broke away from China's Qing Dynasty in 1911 and established independence in 1921 with Soviet military backing, leaving Inner Mongolia inside China. Under Soviet-aligned rule, the 1937–39 Great Repression executed an estimated 22,000 to 35,000 people—including roughly 18,000 Buddhist monks—and destroyed over 700 monasteries before Mongolia transitioned to democracy in 1990.

cards.name: Montenegro
cards.story: An independent mountain principality that fought Ottoman forces for centuries before being absorbed into Yugoslavia in 1918, Montenegro suffered tens of thousands of deaths during World War II's Axis occupation and partisan warfare. Remaining federated with Serbia during Yugoslavia's 1990s breakup—when Montenegrin units took part in shelling Dubrovnik and sheltering tens of thousands of Bosnian and Kosovar refugees—Montenegro voted narrowly in a 2006 referendum to restore independence.

cards.name: Morocco
cards.story: France and Spain forced Morocco into colonial protectorates in 1912 and waged bloody pacification wars—including Spain's use of chemical mustard-gas bombs during the 1920s Rif War—that killed tens of thousands before Morocco regained independence in 1956. In 1975, Morocco militarily occupied most of neighboring Western Sahara, sparking a 16-year war and displacing roughly 170,000 Sahrawi refugees.
cards.contestedNote: Morocco occupies and administers most of Western Sahara as its Southern Provinces, while the UN classifies Western Sahara as a non-self-governing territory whose final status remains unresolved.

cards.name: Mozambique
cards.story: Portugal held coastal slave-trading posts from 1505—trafficking hundreds of thousands of enslaved Africans—and secured Mozambique's colonial borders in the 1890s via forced labor and military subjugation. After a 10-year independence war (1964–74) killed tens of thousands, a brutal 1977–92 civil war backed by white-minority Rhodesia and apartheid South Africa killed roughly 1 million people—mostly through war-induced famine—and displaced over 5 million.

cards.name: Myanmar
cards.story: Britain conquered Burma in three 19th-century wars and forcibly joined central Burman plains with autonomous ethnic borderlands under colonial rule until independence in 1948, igniting the world's longest-running civil wars. In August 2017, Myanmar's military launched genocidal 'clearance operations' in Rakhine State—killing thousands (at least 6,700 in the first month alone) and driving over 740,000 Rohingya refugees into Bangladesh (bringing total displaced Rohingya to ~1 million)—while the 2021 military coup triggered nationwide war displacing over 3.5 million more.
cards.contestedNote: UN investigators have documented genocide and crimes against humanity against the Rohingya (~1 million displaced in Bangladesh) alongside ongoing nationwide civil war following the 2021 military coup.

cards.name: Namibia
cards.story: Germany colonized Namibia in 1884 and, when the Herero and Nama peoples rose against land seizure and brutality in 1904–08, carried out the 20th century's first genocide—driving survivors into the desert and concentration camps and killing 65,000–80,000 Herero (about 80% of the population) and ~10,000 Nama (about 50%). Apartheid South Africa later occupied Namibia for decades, fighting a 23-year liberation war that killed over 20,000 before independence in 1990.

cards.name: Nauru
cards.story: Colonized by Germany in 1888 and later governed by Australia, Britain, and New Zealand, Nauru's interior was strip-mined for phosphate for nearly a century, leaving roughly 80% of the island barren. During World War II, Japan occupied Nauru and forcibly deported 1,200 Nauruans—about two-thirds of the population—to forced labor on Chuuk, where ~463 died before survivors returned and won independence in 1968.

cards.name: Nepal
cards.story: Unified from Himalayan kingdoms by Prithvi Narayan Shah in 1768, Nepal was never colonized by Britain, though defeat in the 1814–16 Anglo-Nepalese War forced the Treaty of Sugauli, stripping roughly a third of its territory to British India. In modern times, the 1996–2006 Maoist civil war killed an estimated 17,000 people and displaced over 100,000 before abolishing the monarchy in 2008.

cards.name: Netherlands
cards.turningPoint: 1648 Peace of Westphalia & 1839 Treaty of London
cards.story: The Dutch Republic won independence from Spain in 1648 after an 80-year war, fixed its European borders in 1839, and endured brutal Nazi WWII occupation—during which ~102,000 Dutch Jews (75% of the community) were murdered in the Holocaust and ~20,000 died in the 1944–45 Hunger Winter. Overseas, the Dutch Empire trafficked roughly 550,000–600,000 enslaved Africans to Suriname and the Caribbean and waged bloody colonial wars in Indonesia killing hundreds of thousands.

cards.name: New Caledonia
cards.story: France annexed New Caledonia in 1853, turning it into a penal colony (~22,000 convicts sent) and seizing over 90% of fertile land from the Indigenous Kanak people—violently crushing Kanak uprisings in 1878 (~1,000+ Kanaks killed) and 1917 while confining survivors to reserves. Pro-independence clashes in the 1980s (including the 1988 Ouvéa cave assault) led to the 1998 Nouméa Accord, though tensions erupted again in 2024 killing over a dozen people.
cards.contestedNote: New Caledonia remains a special collectivity of France; Kanak self-determination movements contest France's constitutional framework, with renewed unrest breaking out in 2024.

cards.name: New Zealand
cards.story: Settled by Polynesian Māori navigators centuries before European arrival, Aotearoa New Zealand entered British rule through the disputed 1840 Treaty of Waitangi. When Māori resisted settler land grabs, British and colonial armies fought the 1845–72 New Zealand Wars—killing ~2,000+ Māori fighters and civilians and confiscating roughly 3.5 million acres of ancestral Māori land—as disease and dispossession cut the Māori population by more than half before New Zealand became a self-governing dominion in 1907.

cards.name: Nicaragua
cards.story: Spanish conquest and slave trading in the 1520s–40s decimated Nicaragua's Indigenous population by over 80% before independence from Spain (1821) and the Central American Federation (1838); Nicaragua forcibly incorporated the autonomous Miskito Coast in 1894. Following U.S. military occupations (1912–33) and the Somoza dictatorship, the 1978–79 Sandinista Revolution and U.S.-backed 1980s Contra War killed an estimated 50,000 to 80,000 Nicaraguans and displaced hundreds of thousands.

cards.name: Niger
cards.story: France conquered Niger in the 1890s through notoriously brutal military expeditions—including the 1899 Voulet-Chanoine mission that massacred thousands and razed entire villages—before drawing colonial borders with Britain that split Hausa and Tuareg homelands. Independent since 1960, recurring Tuareg rebellions and modern Sahel conflicts have displaced hundreds of thousands across its borders.

cards.name: Nigeria
cards.story: Britain conquered historic kingdoms including Benin (sacking and burning the city in 1897) and the Sokoto Caliphate, merging hundreds of ethnic nations into one colony in 1914 after centuries in which roughly 3.5 million enslaved Africans were trafficked from Nigeria's coasts. Seven years after independence in 1960, the Biafran Civil War (1967–70) and federal blockade killed an estimated 1 to 3 million people—predominantly children who starved—and displaced millions.

cards.name: North Korea
cards.story: Unified for over a millennium before brutal Japanese colonial occupation (1910–45)—which conscripted millions of Koreans into forced labor and sexual slavery—Korea was arbitrarily split at the 38th parallel by the U.S. and USSR in 1945. The 1950–53 Korean War devastated the peninsula, killing an estimated 3 to 4 million people (including 2 to 3 million civilians and heavy U.S. bombing that flattened northern cities), displacing roughly 3 million, and permanently separating millions of families across the DMZ.
cards.contestedNote: No peace treaty has ever replaced the 1953 armistice; the Demilitarized Zone remains one of the world's most heavily militarized borders, and both Koreas have historically claimed sovereignty over the entire peninsula.

cards.name: North Macedonia
cards.story: Partitioned among Serbia, Greece, and Bulgaria after the 1912–13 Balkan Wars—accompanied by mass village burnings and displacements—the northern Vardar region became a Yugoslav republic in 1945 (after Bulgarian Axis forces deported over 7,100 Macedonian Jews—98% of the community—to Treblinka in 1943). North Macedonia separated peacefully from Yugoslavia in 1991, navigated a 2001 insurgency that displaced ~170,000 people, and resolved its naming dispute with Greece in 2019.

cards.name: Norway
cards.story: After centuries under Danish and Swedish rule, Norwegians voted overwhelmingly in 1905 to dissolve the union with Sweden peacefully. During World War II, Nazi Germany invaded and occupied Norway (1940–45), deporting ~770 Norwegian Jews to Auschwitz and razing northern Finnmark in a scorched-earth retreat that forcibly evacuated ~50,000 civilians; domestically, Norway's century-long 'Norwegianization' policy forcibly assimilated Indigenous Sámi communities.

cards.name: Oman
cards.story: One of the Arab world's oldest states, Oman built an Indian Ocean maritime empire stretching to Zanzibar—heavily tied to the East African slave trade until Britain pressured its abolition in the late 1800s—while British political advisers exerted deep colonial influence. During the 1963–76 Dhofar Rebellion in southern Oman, British-backed Omani forces suppressed separatist fighters, killing several thousand before border treaties finalized modern desert frontiers.

cards.name: Pakistan
cards.story: Created in August 1947 through Britain's abrupt Partition of India, Pakistan was born amid catastrophic communal violence that killed an estimated 500,000 to 2 million people and forcibly displaced 12 to 18 million across Punjab and Bengal. Originally split into West and East Pakistan separated by India, West Pakistan's brutal 1971 military crackdown in East Pakistan killed hundreds of thousands and drove ~10 million refugees into India before East Pakistan broke away as Bangladesh.
cards.contestedNote: Pakistan and India have fought multiple wars over disputed Kashmir since 1947, divided today along the militarized Line of Control, while Afghanistan has never formally recognized the 1893 colonial Durand Line.

cards.name: Palau
cards.story: Colonized in turn by Spain, Germany, and Japan—under whom epidemics and colonial displacement shrank the Palauan population before World War II's bloody 1944 Battle of Peleliu killed over 12,000 Japanese and U.S. troops and forced Palauans to evacuate—Palau entered a U.S.-run UN Trust Territory. Choosing its own nuclear-free constitution, Palau became fully independent in 1994.

cards.name: Palestine
cards.story: Following the Ottoman Empire's collapse, Britain governed Palestine under a League of Nations mandate until 1948, crushing the 1936–39 Arab Revolt (killing ~5,000 Palestinians). The 1948 war and establishment of Israel triggered the Nakba—forcibly displacing over 700,000 Palestinians and destroying over 400 villages—leaving the West Bank under Jordanian rule and Gaza under Egyptian administration until Israel's 1967 military conquest placed both under occupation and displaced roughly 300,000 more Palestinians; Palestine declared independence in 1988 and became a UN Observer State in 2012.
cards.contestedNote: Recognized as a state by over 140 UN members, Palestine remains under Israeli military occupation, illegal West Bank settlement expansion, and blockade. Since October 2023, Israel's military assault on Gaza—widely described by UN experts and human rights organizations as genocide—has killed over 70,000 Palestinians and displaced the vast majority of Gaza's 2.2 million residents.

cards.name: Panama
cards.story: Spanish conquest decimated Indigenous populations across the isthmus and turned Panama into a transit hub for enslaved Africans and looted Peruvian silver before it became part of Colombia. Backed by U.S. gunboats seeking a canal route, Panama broke from Colombia in 1903—building the Panama Canal at the cost of over 25,000 worker deaths (mostly Afro-Caribbean laborers)—and endured a 1989 U.S. invasion (killing hundreds of civilians) before regaining full control of the Canal Zone in 1999.

cards.name: Papua New Guinea
cards.story: European empires sliced New Guinea down the 141st meridian in the 1880s—Britain and Germany seizing the eastern half (with German colonial plantations using coerced labor and killing hundreds in punitive raids) before Australia took control after World War I; World War II's brutal New Guinea campaign killed over 200,000 Japanese and Allied troops and tens of thousands of Papua New Guineans. Independent since 1975, a 1988–98 civil war and blockade on Bougainville killed an estimated 15,000 to 20,000 people and displaced ~60,000.

cards.name: Paraguay
cards.story: After Spanish colonial missions and conquest reshaped Guaraní lands, Paraguay declared independence in 1811—only to be nearly destroyed in the 1864–70 War of the Triple Alliance against Brazil, Argentina, and Uruguay, which stripped vast territory and killed an estimated 50% to 69% of Paraguay's pre-war population through combat, famine, and disease. A 1932–35 Chaco War with Bolivia killed ~36,000 more Paraguayans before a 1938 treaty secured the Gran Chaco.

cards.name: Peru
cards.story: Spain's 1532–72 conquest of the Inca Empire—alongside Old World epidemics and brutal forced mita labor in silver and mercury mines—collapsed Peru's Indigenous population from ~9–12 million to under 1 million, while colonial Peru also imported ~100,000 enslaved Africans before independence in 1821 and territorial losses to Chile in 1879–84. Between 1980 and 2000, internal war between Shining Path insurgents and state forces killed an estimated 69,000 Peruvians—75% of them Indigenous Quechua speakers—and displaced ~600,000.

cards.name: Philippines
cards.story: Spain colonized over 7,000 islands starting in the 1560s—imposing forced labor and crushing Indigenous and Moro resistance—before ceding the archipelago to the United States in 1898 despite a Filipino independence revolution. In the brutal 1899–1902 Philippine–American War, U.S. forces used reconcentration camps and scorched-earth tactics that killed an estimated 20,000 Filipino fighters and 200,000 to 250,000 civilians (mostly through war-induced famine and cholera); World War II's Japanese occupation and Battle of Manila later killed ~500,000 to 1 million Filipinos before independence in 1946.

cards.name: Poland
cards.story: Partitioned off the map by Russia, Prussia, and Austria in 1795 and reborn in 1918, Poland was invaded simultaneously by Nazi Germany and the USSR in 1939. During World War II, roughly 5.6 to 6 million Polish citizens—nearly 17% of the entire nation, including ~3 million Polish Jews (90% of Poland's Jewish population)—were murdered, and the 1945 Potsdam borders shifted Poland ~150 miles west, forcibly uprooting ~1.5 to 2 million Poles from Soviet-annexed eastern lands and expelling millions of Germans from the west.

cards.name: Portugal
cards.story: Portugal's mainland borders with Spain have barely changed since the 1297 Treaty of Alcañices following the Reconquista—which also led to the 1496–97 forced conversion and expulsion of tens of thousands of Jews and Muslims. Overseas, Portugal pioneered the transatlantic slave trade—trafficking roughly 5.8 million enslaved Africans (nearly half the entire trade, mostly to Brazil)—and waged brutal 1961–74 colonial wars in Angola, Mozambique, and Guinea-Bissau that killed over 100,000 before Portugal's 1974 Carnation Revolution ended its empire.

cards.name: Qatar
cards.story: Consolidating under the Al Thani family in the 1800s, Qatar signed a 1916 British protectorate treaty granting Britain control over its foreign affairs and defense in exchange for maritime protection. When Britain ended its Gulf protectorates in 1971, Qatar chose independent statehood and settled its remaining land and maritime border disputes with Bahrain and Saudi Arabia by 2001.

cards.name: Republic of the Congo
